- **Ilya Sutskever (NeurIPS, December 2024)** said "pretraining as we know it will end," calling data "the fossil fuel of AI."
- **GPT-4.5 (February 2025)** is the clearest public data point.
  - OpenAI described it as roughly an order of magnitude more effective compute than GPT-4.
  - It improved on knowledge, factuality, and conversational quality.
  - It trailed the o-series reasoning models on math and code, was very expensive to serve, and was soon retired from the API.
  - Epoch and others noted the interpretation matters. GPT-3→GPT-4 was roughly 100× compute, while GPT-4→GPT-4.5 was about 10×, so a smaller jump is what scaling laws predict. Part of "diminishing returns" was expecting a GPT-4-sized leap from a tenth of the scale-up.
- **Counterpoint:** Google said Gemini 3 (late 2025) owed substantial gains to improved pretraining as well as post-training, and pushed back on "wall" narratives. Lab statements are not neutral evidence in either direction.

### (c) "Data is becoming the binding constraint." Real, with mitigations.

- Epoch (Villalobos et al.) estimates the effective stock of quality public human text at roughly 100T–1,000T tokens, with ~300T as a central estimate. At current rates that would be fully used sometime around 2026–2032, earlier with heavy overtraining.
- Frontier open-model runs already reported tens of trillions of tokens; Qwen3 reported ~36T.
- Mitigations:
  - **Repetition:** Muennighoff et al. (2023) found up to ~4 epochs is nearly as good as fresh data, with value decaying toward zero by ~16 epochs.
  - **Aggressive quality filtering:** FineWeb-Edu and DCLM showed large gains from curation alone.
  - **Synthetic data** and **multimodal data.**
- How far synthetic data can substitute for human data at the frontier is one of the most important open questions.

**My read:** pretraining returns are diminishing in the economic and marginal sense that matters for lab decisions. Labs shifted compute to RL because it bought more per dollar. That reallocation is not proof the underlying law broke.

There is also an important interaction. Stronger base models appear to be better RL starting points, so pretraining value increasingly shows up *indirectly*, through what RL can extract.

---

## 3. Decomposing the gains: compute, algorithms, data, post-training

| Source | Key evidence | Rough magnitude |
|---|---|---|
| **Physical pretraining compute** | Epoch compute trends | ~4–5×/year; the largest single driver through ~2023 |
| **Algorithmic efficiency (architecture, optimizers, MoE, etc.)** | Ho et al. 2024 (Epoch) | Compute needed for a fixed performance level halves every ~8 months (95% CI ~5–14). Compute scaling still contributed *more* than algorithms over 2012–2023 |
| **Data quality and curation** | Phi series, FineWeb-Edu, DCLM | Often several-fold effective-compute multipliers; mostly *counted inside* the "algorithmic" estimates above |
| **Instruction tuning / RLHF** | InstructGPT 2022 | Labelers preferred a 1.3B InstructGPT over 175B GPT-3, which reflects usability more than raw knowledge |
| **Cheap post-training enhancements** | Davidson et al. 2023 (Epoch) | Fine-tuning, tools, prompting, scaffolding often worth ~5–30× compute-equivalent, at <1% of pretraining cost |
| **RL on verifiable rewards ("reasoning models")** | o1 (2024), DeepSeek-R1 (Jan 2025), o3 | Huge gains in math, competition coding, and science QA (e.g., AIME from low teens to 80–90%+). o3 used ~10× o1's RL compute |
| **Test-time compute** | o1 scaling plots; Snell et al. 2024 | Performance roughly log-linear in reasoning tokens. On suitable problems, a small model with more inference compute can beat a ~14× larger model |

**Notes on individual rows**

- **Algorithms are lumpy and scale-dependent.** Some 2025 work argues much measured algorithmic progress comes from a few innovations whose benefit *grows with scale*, notably the transformer and compute-optimal rebalancing. If so, small-scale ablations understate them and many small tweaks matter little.
- **DeepSeek-V3 illustrates efficiency gains.** It reached roughly GPT-4o-class performance with an estimated ~3×10²⁴ FLOP in its final run, about 2.8M H800 GPU-hours. It combined MoE, attention compression, FP8 training, and multi-token prediction.
- **How much RL creates versus elicits is contested.**
  - Yue et al. (2025) found that at large pass@k, base models often match or beat their RL-tuned versions. On that view, RL mostly *sharpens* sampling toward reasoning the base model can already do.
  - Odd results reinforce the elicitation view: for some model families, even random or spurious rewards improved math scores.
  - Other work, such as prolonged-RL studies, argues extended RL does expand the frontier.
  - Elicitation is still enormously valuable in practice.
- **RL may be less compute-efficient per FLOP than pretraining.** It extracts little information per episode. Toby Ord and Epoch have argued RL compute can't keep growing ~10× every few months, because it is already approaching pretraining scale. xAI said Grok 4's RL compute was close to its pretraining compute.

**Checker ✓, on the decomposition itself**

- **The factors multiply, not add.** RL works better on stronger bases, better data makes architectures look better, and test-time reasoning needs RL-trained models. Any "X% from data" figure depends on the order in which you attribute.
- **Benchmarks are biased toward verifiable domains** (math, code), which is exactly where RL shines. Gains in open-ended writing, judgment, and research taste have been less dramatic and harder to measure. That tilts the apparent attribution toward post-training.
- **Contamination and benchmark saturation** (MMLU near its ceiling) can make progress look either faster or slower than it is.
- **Capability per dollar** has fallen extremely fast, often by an order of magnitude or more per year for a fixed capability level. That is largely distillation, data, and efficiency rather than frontier scale. It is a separate axis from frontier capability.

**A rough period-by-period picture, held loosely:**

- **2019–2023:** mostly pretraining compute, with algorithms and data a strong second (perhaps a third to a half of effective-compute growth), and RLHF converting capability into usefulness.
- **2024–2026:** pretraining compute and data still growing, but marginal *headline* gains disproportionately from:
  - RL post-training;
  - inference-time reasoning;
  - agent scaffolding and tool use;
  - data curation and synthetic data.
- **Agentic task length:** METR's measure of task length AI can complete at 50% reliability doubled about every 7 months over 2019–2025, possibly faster (~4 months) in 2024–2025. That reflects the whole stack, not pretraining alone.

---

## 4. What would sharpen the picture

- **Public loss-versus-compute data from ≥10²⁶ FLOP runs.** This is the direct test of whether the power law is bending.
- **RL scaling curves at larger scale.** Early systematic work (e.g., Meta's 2025 study of RL compute scaling) fits saturating, sigmoid-like curves. Where those ceilings sit, and whether bigger bases raise them, matters a great deal.
- **Synthetic data at the frontier:** whether it extends the data runway or leads to quality collapse.
- **Gains in non-verifiable domains.** If those stay modest while math and code soar, that says RL is doing much of the work and that pretraining's distinct contribution, broad world knowledge and judgment, is what is slowing.

The most defensible single sentence: **scaling laws are an accurate law of pretraining loss and a rough guide to capability growth; returns per dollar from pretraining alone have fallen, but progress continued by opening new scaling axes (RL and inference compute) that each have their own diminishing-returns curves and sit on top of the pretraining base rather than replacing it.**

**Short answer:** Introspection isn't one capacity with one level of reliability. It is reasonably good at reporting what's in your awareness right now, as long as you report promptly and describe rather than explain. It is often poor at what people most want from it: explaining *why* they chose, judged, or felt something, and describing how their minds generally work.

The most important finding isn't that people are sometimes wrong about themselves. It's that made-up self-explanations feel and sound just like accurate ones. Sincerity, detail, and confidence tell you little about whether a self-explanation is true. We have privileged *data* about ourselves (what we attended to, thought, and felt) but little privileged insight into *causes*, and nothing warns us when we start making things up.

## 1. Reasons: the confabulation evidence

**Nisbett & Wilson (1977), "Telling More Than We Can Know."** In a department-store "consumer survey," shoppers judged four pairs of identical nylon stockings. The rightmost pair was preferred over the leftmost by almost four to one. No one mentioned position. When asked directly, virtually everyone denied it mattered, "usually with a worried glance at the interviewer." In a companion study, an instructor's warm or cold manner changed how students rated his appearance, mannerisms, and accent. Students denied this. Some in the cold condition reversed the causal arrow, saying his mannerisms were *why* they disliked him.

The paper's key move was comparing participants' explanations with predictions from observers who only imagined the situation. The two matched, errors included. Nisbett and Wilson concluded that when we explain our behavior, we mostly apply the same shared cultural theories of cause and effect that an outsider would use.
- The explanation is right when the true cause is one the theory flags as plausible.
- It is wrong when the true cause isn't plausible: item position, the number of bystanders present, a warm manner coloring unrelated judgments.

For influences like these, your account of yourself is no better than a stranger's guess. The stranger just knows they're guessing. Nisbett and Wilson drew one important line: people often do know the *content* of their current thoughts and feelings, but not the *processes* that produce their judgments.

**Clinical confabulation shows the explanation system running without input.** In Gazzaniga's split-brain work, a patient's right hemisphere saw a snow scene, and his left hand picked a shovel. His speaking left hemisphere had seen only a chicken claw. It explained instantly: "you need a shovel to clean out the chicken shed." Stroke patients who deny that their left arm is paralyzed say they're tired or don't feel like moving it. These patients aren't lying, and their inventions feel as authoritative to them as true reports. Gazzaniga called this system the "interpreter." In healthy people it has better information, so its stories are usually closer to the truth, but nothing marks when it's guessing.

**Healthy people do it in consequential decisions.** Evaluators choosing between a man and a woman for a construction job or a police-chief post favored the man. Whichever credential he had, education or experience, became the one they said mattered most (Norton et al., 2004; Uhlmann & Cohen, 2005, who called this "constructed criteria"). They sincerely believed they were judging on merit. Committing to criteria *before* seeing the candidates eliminated the bias. Related work found that making people feel objective *increased* biased hiring.

**A counterweight.** Haidt's famous "moral dumbfounding" demonstration has held up less well. In it, people condemned harmless sibling incest and then said "I just know it's wrong." A re-analysis found many participants never accepted the premise that no harm could result (Royzman et al., 2015). Condemnation without reasons happens, but less often than the story suggests. Sometimes the stated reasons really are the operative ones.

## 2. Choice blindness

Johansson, Hall and colleagues (2005) had people pick the more attractive of two faces, then handed them the chosen card and asked why. On some trials, sleight of hand gave them the face they had *rejected*.
- About three-quarters of these switches went undetected, even when people had unlimited time to decide.
- People then explained choices they hadn't made, sometimes citing features the face they'd actually picked didn't have, such as earrings.
- Explanations for switched and genuine choices were about equally detailed, emotional, and confident.

The effect extends well beyond faces:

- **Taste and smell:** in a supermarket, fewer than a third of switches between jams or teas were caught. This held even for pairs as different as cinnamon-apple and bitter grapefruit (Hall et al., 2010).
- **Moral and political views:** on a survey rigged so some answers were secretly reversed, about two-thirds of people endorsed and argued for at least one position opposite to what they'd just given (Hall et al., 2012). In a version run before a Swedish election, most accepted altered answers, and some shifted their voting intentions.
- **Your own words and arguments:** people who heard a different word in their own voice through headphones often accepted that they'd said it (Lind et al., 2014). People shown their own earlier arguments, disguised as someone else's, often rejected them (Trouche et al., 2016).
- **The confabulation becomes true:** after defending a switched face, people later preferred it (Johansson et al., 2014).
- **Choice-blindness blindness:** most participants who missed every switch were confident they would have noticed one.

Interpret this carefully:
- In the lab you have a strong, reasonable prior that the card in your hand is the one you picked. Accepting it can be sensible inference, not proof that you lack access to your choice.
- Detection tends to rise for more dissimilar options and for strongly held attitudes.
- Some participants may notice but not say so.
- One small study used a careful interview that walked people back through the moment of choice. It reported substantially higher detection (Petitmengin et al., 2013).

What choice blindness establishes is narrower but still striking. The system that explains your choices can produce a fluent, confident explanation without access to the actual choice. And your sense that you'd catch a mismatch is inflated.

## 3. Introspecting changes what you're looking at

Introspection is often an intervention, not a passive reading. Timothy Wilson and colleagues found that listing reasons for a preference changes the preference:

- Students who analyzed why they liked various jams gave ratings that correlated about .11 with expert rankings. Students who just tasted correlated about .55 (Wilson & Schooler, 1991).
- People who analyzed reasons chose different posters and were less satisfied with them weeks later.
- Dating partners who analyzed their relationship gave attitudes that no longer predicted whether they'd still be together months later.

The proposed mechanism: verbalizing pulls attention toward features that are easy to put into words, which may not be what drives your preferences. You then temporarily adopt the attitude those reasons imply. These are older, small-sample studies, so treat the effect sizes skeptically. But the theme recurs elsewhere. Explaining your thinking, as opposed to just voicing it, changes how you solve problems. And defending a choice in choice-blindness studies reshapes the preference.

## 4. Feelings

**Reasonably reliable: how you feel right now, reported in the moment.** Experience-sampling data are coherent, and for pain there's no better measure than asking. Overall life-satisfaction ratings are also sturdier than critics once claimed:
- The well-known finding that weather sways them vanished in a sample of over a million people (Lucas & Lawless, 2013).
- Question-order effects turn out to be small.
- Self-ratings agree moderately with ratings from friends and family.

**Systematically biased:**

- **Remembered feelings.** Retrospective judgments track the peak and the end of an experience, not its length. In Kahneman's cold-water study, about two-thirds of people chose to repeat a *longer* painful episode because its final stretch was slightly less cold. Memories of past attitudes and emotions also drift toward present ones.
- **Predicted feelings.** People overestimate how intense and lasting future emotions will be.
- **Causes of feelings.** Expectations change the experience itself. Wine labeled expensive tastes better, with matching brain activity (Plassmann et al., 2008), and people credit the wine. The textbook evidence that we label vague physical arousal based on context (Schachter and Singer's adrenaline study, the shaky-bridge study) is weaker than usually presented.
- **Labeling and bodily sensing.** People differ widely in how finely they distinguish emotions. Beliefs about how well you sense your own heartbeat correlate only weakly with measured accuracy (Garfinkel et al., 2015).

So "How do I feel?" is answerable. Self-knowledge degrades with "Why do I feel this?", "How did that feel?" asked months later, and "How will I feel?"

## 5. Mental processes and the texture of experience

**You see outputs, not processes.**
- Blindsight patients deny seeing, yet point to targets well above chance.
- People come to prefer shapes they were shown before, even when they don't recognize them.
- Even *when* you decided can be reconstructed afterward. In Libet-style tasks, people report the moment they felt the urge to move. A magnetic pulse to the brain or a delayed tone, delivered *after* the movement, shifts that reported moment (Lau et al., 2007; Banks & Isham, 2009).
- The feeling of authorship can be missing even when you are the author. In "facilitated communication," facilitators sincerely believed the messages came from the nonspeaking people they assisted. Double-blind tests showed the facilitators produced them.

**Beliefs about your own inner life are often wrong.** Russell Hurlburt's Descriptive Experience Sampling uses random beeps, followed by careful interviews about the moment just before each beep.
- Inner speech shows up in roughly a quarter of samples on average.
- Some people who are sure they narrate constantly have almost none.
- Many discover "unsymbolized thinking," thought without words or images, which they hadn't believed existed.

Eric Schwitzgebel collects more examples:
- People believe their visual field is detailed far into the periphery. Yet they can't tell whether a playing card held off to the side is red or black until it's surprisingly close to where they're looking.
- Mid-century Americans mostly reported dreaming in black and white, and that report faded as color film and TV spread. Whether the dreams or the reports changed is still debated, and that we can't easily tell is part of the point.
- People greatly overestimate how much visual change they'd notice, a finding called "change blindness blindness."

Hurlburt thinks careful reports of specific moments can be trusted; Schwitzgebel doubts even those. Some reports clearly track something real, though. People who report no visual imagery (aphantasia) also lack imagery's measurable effects on binocular rivalry and pupil size.

## 6. Where introspection does work

- **Real-time, descriptive reports.** Ericsson and Simon's research, supported by a 2011 meta-analysis, shows that thinking aloud yields valid data on the sequence of thoughts. Here, thinking aloud means voicing what's in mind without explaining it. It barely changes accuracy, though it slows people down. Much of Nisbett and Wilson's evidence involved reports, after the fact, about influences people were never attending to.
- **Confidence.** For most people, confidence tracks accuracy well above chance. How well it does varies between individuals, and that variation relates to differences in prefrontal brain structure (Fleming et al., 2010). But confidence is inferred from cues like ease of processing, so misleading cues fool it. Words in a larger font feel more memorable without being so.
- **Some traits.** Your own ratings beat friends' ratings for internal, hard-to-see traits like anxiety. Friends do better for visible, evaluative traits like intelligence (Vazire, 2010). Across many meta-analyses, self-assessed ability correlates about .3 with measured performance: real, but weak.
- **"Unconscious" attitudes.** People predict their own implicit-association-test results fairly well (Hahn et al., 2014). Implicit attitudes are less hidden than often claimed.
- **Training.** Feedback modestly improves how well confidence tracks accuracy. Structured interviewing also recovers more than casual self-report.

## 7. What seems to be going on

The converging view is that much of what feels like looking inward is actually inference. It's the same mind-reading we apply to other people, run on richer data. That explains Nisbett and Wilson's finding that self-explanations matched observers' guesses: you and the observer are using the same theory.
- Bem's self-perception theory proposed that we infer our attitudes partly from watching our own behavior.
- Developmental evidence fits. Three-year-olds who can't yet grasp that others can hold false beliefs make the same error about their own past beliefs. After discovering pencils in a candy box, they insist they thought it held pencils all along (Gopnik & Astington, 1988).
- Peter Carruthers argues we have fairly direct access to sensory-like states: images, inner speech, bodily feelings. Our judgments, decisions, and reasons, by contrast, are interpreted from those cues and from behavior.

The crucial problem is that inferences don't come labeled as inferences. A guess about why you acted arrives feeling like an observation. So confabulation isn't a rare malfunction. It's the normal operation of an explanation system that has no reliable "I don't know" signal.

Emily Pronin's work on the "introspection illusion" adds a corollary. People judge their own bias by consulting their thoughts, where bias rarely shows. They judge others' bias by behavior. The result is that people see bias everywhere except in themselves.

Why would we have such a system? Two theories:
- Mercier and Sperber argue that reasoning evolved largely to justify ourselves to others and to evaluate their arguments. That predicts fluent self-justification and lax scrutiny of our own reasons.
- Fiery Cushman argues that rationalization can be useful. Inventing the beliefs and desires that would explain your behavior turns implicit tendencies into explicit ideas you can plan with.

Both are theories, and they are less settled than the data.

## 8. How the evidence gets overstated

- **Selected failures.** The classic studies deliberately used influences people wouldn't think of. They show *that* and *how* introspection fails, not how often it fails in daily life. If you say you left a party because you were bored, you're probably right. That's not because you perceived the cause directly, but because you have a decent theory plus data no observer has.
- **Replication.** Several popular "puppets of trivial cues" findings have collapsed or shrunk:
  - behavioral priming
  - claimed advantages of "unconscious thought"
  - the original pen-in-mouth facial-feedback effect
  - weather effects on life satisfaction

  The core findings here have held up reasonably well, often with smaller effects than first reported: position effects, choice blindness, clinical confabulation, peak-end effects, emotional forecasting errors, and weak self-assessment.
- **Lab artificiality.** Trusting the experimenter is rational, and real decisions usually involve higher stakes and more feedback.

## Scorecard

| What you're reporting | Reliability | Representative evidence |
|---|---|---|
| What's in mind right now, voiced as it happens | Fairly good | Think-aloud research |
| Current pain or mood | Decent; often the best measure available | Experience sampling |
| Confidence in a judgment you just made | Moderate, depends on cues | Research on confidence and accuracy |
| Why you chose, judged, or felt something | Often poor for subtle causes; tracks plausibility, not access | Nisbett & Wilson; choice blindness; constructed criteria |
| How your mind generally works | Often poor | Hurlburt; Schwitzgebel |
| How often you do things | Moderate (self-reported vs. logged phone use, r ≈ .4) | Behavior-logging studies |
| Past feelings and attitudes | Systematically biased | Peak-end effect; drift toward current views |
| Future feelings | Systematically biased | Emotional forecasting research |
| Abilities and evaluative traits | Weak (r ≈ .3) | Self-assessment meta-analyses |

Rule of thumb: introspection works better for *what* than *why*, for *now* than *then*, and for *describing* than *generalizing*. It also works better when your self-image has nothing riding on the answer.

## Practical implications

- **Record in the moment.** Notes written during an experience beat later reconstructions.
- **Treat your "why" as a hypothesis.** If a stranger would have guessed the same explanation, it may be theory rather than perception. Test it where you can: taste blind, reorder the options, ask whether you'd still choose the same way without the reason you cited.
- **Set criteria before seeing the options,** in hiring, purchasing, and grading.
- **Use outside data:** logs for habits, trusted people for visible and ego-relevant traits.
- **Don't check for your own bias by looking inward.** Look at your choices.
- **Be most suspicious of explanations that arrive instantly, fluently, and flatteringly.**
- **"I don't know why" is often the accurate answer.** It's worth tolerating rather than filling in.

One last note, since you're asking an AI: the same caution applies to me. My descriptions of how I reached an answer are produced the same way as the rest of my text. They aren't a direct readout of the underlying computation.
- Interpretability research at Anthropic caught a model explaining that it added two numbers with the schoolbook carry-the-one method, when its internal mechanism worked quite differently.
- Reasoning models' written chains of thought often omit hints that demonstrably changed their answers, much like the shoppers who never mentioned position.
- Experiments that inject concepts directly into a model's internal activity found some genuine but narrow and unreliable ability to notice them.

So treat my self-reports the way this research suggests treating anyone's: as informative hypotheses, not readouts.

Each of the three captures something true about the brain, and each becomes misleading once it's taken as the whole story. If I had to choose, I'd pick "something else": the brain as a **living control organ**. My main reason is that this framing explains why the other three work where they do. Three features of your question matter more than the pick itself:

1. The frameworks mostly answer **different questions at different levels**, so "which is it really?" is partly a malformed question.
2. They still **genuinely collide** at a few seams, and those collisions are empirical, not matters of taste.
3. The deepest cost of commitment is that a framework doesn't just explain data. It decides what counts as **noise**. What you lose is mostly invisible, because it has been filed there.

**The track record.** The brain has been modeled as hydraulics (Descartes), clockwork, a telegraph network, a telephone switchboard and a digital computer. Each time it was the most impressive technology of the day (Matthew Cobb's *The Idea of the Brain* traces the sequence). Each metaphor captured something real and was retired for what it hid. So it's worth noticing that "prediction machine" became dominant in exactly the decades when prediction-trained machines became our most impressive technology. Two caveats keep this from being a debunking. Helmholtz called perception unconscious inference in the 1860s. And "computation" and "dynamics" are mathematical abstractions, not technologies, so they're less tied to an era than the switchboard was. The lesson isn't that today's frameworks are wrong. It's that they're lenses, and lenses have blind spots.

### 1. The computer

The word carries two very different claims.

**The strong claim** is that the brain works like the machines we build. That claim is dead:
- There's no central clock, no separation of memory from processing, and no hardware/software divide. In a brain, running the "program" rewrites the "hardware."
- Wiring doesn't even fix function. Eve Marder's work on the crab stomatogastric ganglion shows one small circuit producing different rhythms under different neuromodulators, and near-identical rhythms from very different underlying parameters.
- We've had the *C. elegans* wiring diagram since 1986 and still can't simply read the worm's behavior off it.

**The abstract claim** is that the brain *computes*: it transforms information in ways that can be described independently of the substrate. Much of cognitive neuroscience's success lives here. Marr's levels gave the field a research program: what problem is solved and why, by what algorithm and representations, in what physical implementation. And some neural representations aren't just attributed by experimenters; the brain causally *uses* them:
- Microstimulating direction-tuned neurons in area MT biases a monkey's judgment of motion direction (Salzman, Britten & Newsome, 1990).
- Hippocampal place-cell sequences sweep out paths to remembered goals before the animal takes them (Pfeiffer & Foster, 2013).
- Networks trained only to recognize objects turn out to predict neural responses along the primate ventral stream (Yamins, DiCarlo and colleagues).

**What it costs.**
- **Time.** A computation's logic cares about *order*. Brains care about *timing* almost everywhere.
- **Chemistry, metabolism and the body.**
- **The brain's own ongoing activity.** The input → process → output picture treats a brain as idle until stimulated. In fact, stimulus-evoked activity is a small perturbation on enormous intrinsic activity (what Raichle called the brain's "dark energy").
- **A blurred distinction.** Talk of neural "codes" quietly merges two claims: *this activity correlates with the stimulus* and *the brain uses this activity as a stand-in for it*. Many confusions live in that gap (Brette, 2019).
- **Triviality.** Under loose criteria, everything computes. All the content lies in *which* computation, in *what* medium. Neural computation may be neither digital nor analog but a kind of its own (Piccinini & Bahar, 2013).

*Failure mode when taken as the whole story:* mind-as-software. This produces upload fantasies, disembodiment and brain-training hype.

### 2. The prediction machine

Predictive processing says the brain continuously generates its best guess about the causes of its inputs and corrects that guess using prediction error.
- Perception is the guess (a "controlled hallucination," as Clark and Seth put it).
- Action is making the guess come true.
- Attention is weighting errors by their expected reliability ("precision").
- Learning is revising the model.

**What it buys.** Genuine unification. It explains:
- why cortex is drenched in feedback connections;
- why expectation reshapes what you see;
- why you can't tickle yourself (the predicted consequences of your own movement get dampened; Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith);
- why mouse visual cortex responds when the visual scene stops matching the animal's running (Keller and colleagues).

It has also helped make psychiatry computational. Hallucination-like percepts can be conditioned in the lab and modeled as over-weighted prior expectations (Powers, Mathys & Corlett, 2017). And it brought the body back in. Interoceptive prediction, meaning the brain anticipating the states of heart, gut and immune system, is now a serious account of emotion and selfhood (Barrett; Seth).

**What it costs.**
- **Flexibility.** The unification is partly bought this way. If priors and precisions can be set after the fact, almost anything fits; Bowers & Davis called these "Bayesian just-so stories."
- **A category slip at the top.** The grand form, Friston's free-energy principle as a theory of all self-organizing life and mind, is better read as a formal modeling framework than as an empirical hypothesis. Its defenders compare it to variational principles in physics, which is fair. But then it can't also be counted as an empirical discovery.
- **Mixed circuit evidence.** The circuit-level story (dedicated prediction and error units in particular cortical layers) is not settled. Expectation sometimes dampens sensory responses and sometimes sharpens them; Press, Kok & Yon (2020) call this the "perceptual prediction paradox." The theory has room for both, which is either sophistication or slack depending on whom you ask.
- **Means/end slippage, the most important cost.** Prediction is plausibly the brain's main *strategy*, but organisms aren't trying to minimize surprise. They're trying to stay alive. This is the "dark room problem": why not sit in the dark forever, where nothing surprises you? The standard answer is that creatures like us *expect* to be fed, which quietly brings the organism's needs back in.
- **Internalism.** Some versions seal the mind behind a statistical boundary (a Markov blanket), which sits badly with how much cognition leans on body and world.

The practical move: keep the local, testable models, and treat the grand principle as a modeling language rather than a finding.

*Failure mode:* "reality is a hallucination." A careful technical claim turns into pop solipsism.

### 3. The dynamical system

Every physical system is a dynamical system, so the substantive claim isn't about what the brain *is*. It's that state spaces, trajectories, attractors and bifurcations are the right *vocabulary*.

**What it buys.** Time becomes central, and some long-running debates dissolve. The best case is motor cortex. For decades, researchers argued about what its neurons "encode": force, direction, velocity, or muscle activity. Churchland, Shenoy and colleagues reframed the question. Preparatory activity sets the starting state of a dynamical system, and the unfolding of that system *generates* the movement. One of their paper titles asks: "representation of movement or first cog in a dynamical machine?" For many in the field, "what does it represent?" turned out to be a question imposed by the lens rather than the data, though the specific findings on rotating population activity still have critics.

The same vocabulary handles:
- sudden transitions in coordination (the Haken–Kelso–Bunz model of finger-wagging);
- development (Thelen and Smith's dynamical account of infants' A-not-B error);
- attractor models of memory and decision;
- a literal ring of neurons tracking heading in the fruit fly brain (Kim et al., 2017).

It has improved brain–computer interface decoding. And it treats brain, body and world as one coupled system without first having to draw a boundary.

**What it costs.**
- **Content and correctness.** A trajectory isn't true or false. A dynamical description of seeing and of misseeing can look alike unless you import something like representation.
- **Reach.** It has far less traction on compositional cognition: language, abstract reasoning, symbolic planning.
- **Overfitting.** Low-dimensional fits can be elegant descriptions that don't generalize.

The field's working synthesis, "computation through neural population dynamics" (Vyas et al., 2020), is a bridge rather than a victory. It treats dynamics as the *medium* in which computation happens.

*Failure mode:* vague holism, where "it's a complex system" ends the conversation.

### 4. Something else

**A living control organ.** Brains evolved to coordinate movement and regulate a body. Supporting lines of work include:
- Wolpert's argument that brains exist to produce adaptable movement;
- Sterling's and Barrett's *allostasis*, the anticipatory regulation of the body's resources;
- Cisek's program of rebuilding our functional categories from evolutionary history.

What persuades me is that this framing explains *why the other three fit where they do*:
- **Prediction.** Conant and Ashby's 1970 "good regulator" theorem says an optimal regulator must embody a model of the system it regulates. The theorem is narrower than its slogan, but suggestive: regulation entails modeling. Neural delays of around a hundred milliseconds also mean a controller in a moving world must anticipate rather than react.
- **Computation.** Regulation is information processing.
- **Dynamics.** The controller is coupled to a body and a world.

On this reading, keeping a body viable is the *job*, prediction is the *strategy*, computation describes *what is achieved*, and dynamics is the *physics*.

Its costs are real. There's a just-so risk, because a story about what something is "for" can be told about anything. And it struggles to explain mathematics, music and metaphysics without a lot of hand-waving about traits repurposed from other uses.

**An evolved kludge.** This is less a rival theory than a warning to all of them. The brain is a layered historical artifact, and our categories (perception, attention, memory, decision) come from folk psychology, not neuroanatomy. Buzsáki's "inside-out" critique argues we've been hunting neural correlates of categories that may not be natural kinds.

**Not just the brain.** Embodied and enactive views argue the unit of analysis is brain, body and world together. You can't understand reaching without the arm's mechanics, or emotion without the viscera.

### 5. Where they actually collide

These are the seams where commitment has testable consequences:

- **Representation.** Are there internal states that stand in for things and are *used* as such? The evidence points to a local answer. Motor cortex looks more like a pattern generator; hippocampus and MT look robustly representational. The brain may not be one kind of thing, so commit region by region and task by task, not globally.
- **One principle or many.** Unification only counts if it costs something: risky predictions, fixed in advance, that rivals don't make. Otherwise it's what critics call "unification by fiat" (Litwin & Miłkowski, 2020).
- **The boundary.** Is the system the brain, the brain plus body, or brain, body and world? This decides what you measure, which decides what you can ever find.

### 6. What commitment buys and costs

- **You can't maximize everything.** Richard Levins argued in 1966 that a model can't simultaneously maximize generality, realism and precision. The free-energy principle maximizes generality. Detailed biophysical models maximize realism. A dynamical model of reaching maximizes precision. Committing to a framework *is* choosing which virtue to give up.
- **Every framework defines its noise.** Spontaneous activity was noise for the input–output view; it's the main event for dynamical and predictive views. Trial-to-trial variability was noise; some now read it as the brain sampling from probability distributions (Orbán et al., 2016). Neuromodulators were background until Marder showed they reconfigure circuits. The body was peripheral until allostasis made it central. Each correction came from someone working in a different frame.
- **Refusing to commit isn't an option either.** Jonas and Kording (2017) applied standard neuroscience methods (lesions, tuning curves, correlations) to a simulated 1970s microprocessor running *Donkey Kong*. The methods failed to reveal how it worked. Data don't organize themselves into understanding; you need a level of description. And hedging across frameworks never pushes any one of them far enough to find its edges.
- **An odd witness.** I'm a system literally implemented on a computer and trained largely on prediction. Yet knowing that tells you remarkably little about how I do what I do. Interpretability researchers have had to build new levels of description: features, circuits, representational geometry. Being implemented on X doesn't make X the best explanatory level, for brains or for me. Systems like me also press on the control view, because prediction without a body to regulate yields a lot of competence. That suggests we've been bundling two questions: what brains are *for*, and what intelligent behavior *requires*. A framework that answers one shouldn't get credit for the other.

So my recommendation: **commit as a method, not as a belief about what the brain is.** Push a framework as hard as it will go. But keep a written list of what it files as noise, and of what result would make you retreat. Prefer "for purpose P, at level L, X is the most productive description" to "the brain *is* X."

### Where each claim stands

| Lens | Modest claim | Grand claim | What would hurt it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Computer** | The brain computes, and some neural states are representations it *uses*: **well-founded** where tested | The brain works like the computers we build: **refuted** | Supposed representations that can be decoded but are never causally used |
| **Prediction machine** | Learned expectation shapes perception and action throughout: **well-founded**. Dedicated error/prediction circuits: **contested** | Free-energy minimization as the principle of all life and mind: **a formal framework, not a testable hypothesis** | Pre-registered tests where it and simpler accounts diverge, with precisions fixed in advance |
| **Dynamical system** | Population dynamics as the medium of neural computation: **well-supported**, especially in motor systems | Cognition needs no representations: **overreach** | Fits that don't generalize; no traction on compositional thought |
| **Living control organ** | Brains evolved for movement and bodily regulation: **defensible** | All cognition is regulation and requires a living body: **contested** | Rich competence fully decoupled from regulation, which machines partly show |

### Bottom line

If forced to compress: **the brain is a living control organ. Its job is to keep a body viable and acting well in its world, by anticipating rather than merely reacting.** "Computer" names what it achieves, in a medium unlike any computer we've built. "Prediction machine" names its main strategy, at least in cortex. "Dynamical system" names how it physically unfolds.

That's a bet about what brains are *for*. Whether minds *require* any of it is a separate question, and machines like me are a live, unresolved data point there. None of the four explains why any of this is *experienced*. A framework that claims to has smuggled the answer in somewhere.

# How Much Do We Know About the Origin of Life?

**Short answer:** We know a fair amount about *when* life started and *what the endpoint looked like*. There is also a large body of solid lab chemistry showing that many individual ingredients form without biology. What we don't have is a continuous, demonstrated path from simple geochemistry to a system that replicates, varies, and evolves on its own, under one geologically realistic set of conditions. The parts list is in decent shape. How the parts were assembled is not known.

---

## 1. The constraints (fairly solid)

**Timing.** Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago (Ga). Zircon crystals suggest liquid water by about 4.4 Ga.
- **Strong evidence:** stromatolites and microbial textures in Western Australia at about 3.48–3.43 Ga. These include what look like land-based hot-spring deposits.
- **Contested evidence:** older claims, including 3.7 Ga Isua stromatolites, 3.77–4.28 Ga "microfossils," and isotopically light carbon in a 4.1 Ga zircon.
- **Molecular clocks:** a 2024 analysis (Moody et al.) put the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) at about 4.2 Ga. That figure has wide error bars and is debated.

The robust takeaway is that life appeared geologically quickly, within a few hundred million years of habitable conditions and possibly much less.

**The endpoint (LUCA).** Comparing modern genomes, we can reconstruct an ancestor that already had:
- DNA, RNA, and ribosomes
- the nearly universal genetic code
- ATP synthase, and probably carbon fixation chemistry related to the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway

Recent estimates give it perhaps a couple thousand protein families. So LUCA was a sophisticated organism, not the first cell. Everything between the first replicator and LUCA is largely invisible to us.

**Molecular fossils.** Modern biology carries strong hints of an earlier RNA-dominated stage:
- The ribosome's catalytic core, the peptidyl transferase center, is RNA, not protein.
- Many core cofactors (ATP, NAD, FAD, coenzyme A) are built from nucleotides.

This is real evidence, not just a story.

---

## 2. A step-by-step ledger

| Step | What has been shown | What's missing | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Amino acids** | Miller–Urey (1953) and successors, including in less reducing atmospheres. Dozens of amino acids in meteorites. 14 of the 20 protein amino acids in samples from asteroid Bennu. | Little; this is the easy part | **High** |
| **Nucleobases** | Adenine from cyanide chemistry (Oró, 1960). All five bases found in meteorites and Bennu samples. | Pyrimidine yields under natural conditions | **High** (purines), **moderate** (pyrimidines) |
| **Sugars** | Formose reaction makes ribose; borate minerals can stabilize it. Ribose reported in meteorites and, recently, Bennu. | Formose gives a messy tar where ribose is minor; selectivity | **Moderate–low** |
| **Nucleotides** | Powner, Gerland & Sutherland (2009) made pyrimidine nucleotides by bypassing free ribose. Carell's group (2019) gave a joint pyrimidine/purine route via wet–dry cycles. Sutherland's "cyanosulfidic" network makes nucleotide, amino acid, and lipid precursors from HCN and H₂S with UV light. | Sequential steps, purification, specific timing; are the conditions geologically realistic? | **Moderate** |
| **Phosphorus** | Meteoritic schreibersite; phosphite; carbonate-rich lakes concentrating phosphate (Toner & Catling 2020); prebiotic phosphorylating agents like diamidophosphate | Which source actually mattered | **Moderate** |
| **Amphiphiles and vesicles** | Fatty acids from mineral-catalyzed synthesis and in meteorites. These self-assemble into vesicles that grow and divide (Szostak lab). | Path to phospholipids; stability in salty or Mg²⁺-rich water | **High** for vesicles, **low** for the path to modern membranes |
| **Polymers** | Short peptides and depsipeptides from wet–dry cycling. RNA oligomers up to ~50 nucleotides on montmorillonite clay with activated nucleotides (Ferris 1996). | Long, specific sequences; a plausible activation chemistry | **Moderate** for short, **low** for long |
| **Nonenzymatic RNA copying** | Template-directed copying with 2-aminoimidazole-activated nucleotides works for short templates (Szostak lab) | Fidelity, sequence bias, and especially strand separation: products stay stuck to templates. No complete multi-generation cycle. | **Low–moderate** |
| **Catalytic and replicating RNA** | Ribozymes are real (Cech, Altman). In vitro evolution yields new catalysts easily. Cross-catalytic ligase pairs amplify exponentially and compete (Lincoln & Joyce 2009), but are fed pre-made pieces. Polymerase ribozymes (Bartel → Holliger → Joyce labs) now make long products and other functional ribozymes, and have driven a crude Darwinian evolution of another ribozyme (Joyce lab 2024). Recent reports describe small polymerases copying segments of themselves at low yield under specialized conditions. | A ribozyme that replicates itself efficiently and repeatedly from plausible monomers | **Partial, advancing** |
| **Protometabolism** | Metal- and mineral-catalyzed reactions resembling glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and Krebs-cycle chemistry (Ralser, Moran). H₂ + CO₂ → formate, acetate, pyruvate on Ni–Fe minerals (Preiner et al. 2020). Iron–sulfur clusters forming with peptides under UV. | A self-sustaining, autocatalytic network that also carries heritable information | **Partial** |
| **Protocells** | RNA copying inside fatty-acid vesicles, using citrate to protect membranes from Mg²⁺. Vesicles with more RNA can outcompete neighbors for lipid. Coacervate droplets support ribozyme activity. | Genuine coupling of genetic function to compartment growth and division | **Partial** |
| **Translation and the genetic code** | Ribozymes can attach amino acids to RNA. Fragments of the ribosome's core can promote peptide-bond formation. RNA–peptide chimeras from modified nucleosides (Carell 2022). The code is strongly error-minimizing (Freeland & Hurst). | How a coded system arose at all | **Very low** |
| **Integration into an evolving cell** | Nothing end-to-end | Essentially everything | **Unknown** |

---

## 3. The genuinely open problems

**1. The continuity problem.** Successful syntheses often need different, sometimes incompatible conditions: UV-lit surface pools for cyanosulfidic chemistry, H₂-rich alkaline vents for CO₂ reduction, freezing or drying cycles for concentration. Many routes also require a chemist to add purified reagents in a specific order.

Critics call this "the chemist's hand." Defenders argue that geology provides sequential processing: flowing streams, evaporation, impacts, hot springs. Two main camps:
- **Vent camp** (Russell, Martin, Lane): emphasizes natural redox and pH gradients. Direct experimental support for gradient-driven chemistry exists (Hudson et al. 2020) but is modest.
- **Surface pond/hot-spring camp** (Sutherland, Deamer, Damer): has stronger synthetic chemistry, and the 3.48 Ga hot-spring evidence is suggestive.

Neither has a complete pathway. A hybrid scenario involving multiple environments, with meteoritic delivery as a supplement, is quite possible.

**2. Bootstrapping heredity.** Darwinian evolution requires replication accurate enough to preserve information. Eigen's paradox is that without an accurate replicase you can't maintain a long genome, but you need a long genome to encode an accurate replicase.

Strand separation, error rates, and "parasites" (short sequences that get copied without contributing) are serious obstacles. Theory and some experiments show that compartments or spatial structure can suppress parasites. Still, nobody has a self-sustaining genetic system starting from simple monomers. This is arguably the central gap.

**3. Homochirality.** Life uses left-handed amino acids and right-handed sugars. Amplification mechanisms are well demonstrated: autocatalysis (the Soai reaction), crystallization-based symmetry breaking, and spin-selective crystallization on magnetite (Sasselov group). Small enantiomeric excesses exist in meteorites. Which mechanism actually seeded the bias, and whether it came before or emerged during early evolution, is unresolved.

**4. The origin of translation and the genetic code.** This may be the deepest mystery. Protein synthesis requires a ribosome, transfer RNAs, and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (themselves proteins), all coordinated by a code mapping triplets to amino acids. Competing explanations include:
- chemical affinities between codons and amino acids (stereochemical theory)
- the code expanding alongside amino-acid biosynthesis (coevolution theory)
- selection for error-tolerance
- a "frozen accident"

There are suggestive fragments, such as "urzyme" cores of synthetases (Carter) and proto-ribosome models, but no experimental route to a working coded system.

**5. From protocell to LUCA.** We don't know how cells transitioned from fatty acids to phospholipids. Archaea and bacteria use chemically different, opposite-handed membrane lipids, which makes LUCA's own membrane a puzzle. We also don't know how chemiosmotic energy coupling arose, or how DNA took over from RNA. This interval likely spans substantial evolution and possibly much horizontal gene transfer, and it has left little trace.

**6. How likely was it?** Early appearance hints that abiogenesis may not be extremely improbable. But we have exactly one example, and observer-selection effects weaken the inference. We know all known life shares one ancestor. We don't know whether life started once or several times, with only one lineage surviving.

---

## 4. Reading headlines skeptically

- **"Building blocks of life found on asteroid X"** is real and interesting chemistry. It shows that organic synthesis is cosmically common. It doesn't address replication, coding, or organization.
- **"Prebiotically plausible"** is a judgment call. Check yields, concentrations, purity, and whether the conditions are mutually compatible with neighboring steps.
- **"Self-replicating molecule created"** usually means replication from pre-made, activated fragments, or a few generations at low yield. That is meaningful progress, but it is not open-ended evolution from simple feedstocks.

---

## 5. What would change the picture

- **A lab system that undergoes open-ended Darwinian evolution**, built from feedstocks that geology could plausibly supply. This is the decisive experiment, and several groups are converging on pieces of it.
- **A second, independent origin**: life in the subsurface of Mars, or in the oceans of Enceladus or Europa, with biochemistry that is clearly not related to ours. That would tell us abiogenesis isn't a fluke. Finding nothing in good habitats would also be informative.
- **Better Hadean geology**, especially firmer constraints on early atmosphere composition, phosphate availability, and land surfaces.

---

### Three lenses on it

Since your project frames problems through Weaver, Maker, and Checker, here's the compressed version through each:

- **Weaver (pattern):** The most striking signal is convergence. Core metabolism, nucleotide cofactors, and the RNA heart of the ribosome all look like they follow chemistry's natural grain rather than arbitrary design. That makes the problem feel tractable.
- **Maker (what to build):** The bottleneck isn't more building blocks. It's demonstrating one integrated, self-sustaining, evolving system.
- **Checker (what could be wrong):** Nearly every "solved" step was solved in isolation, under curated conditions. The honest state of the field is strong chemistry for the parts, real but partial progress on replication and compartments, and genuine ignorance about coding and integration.

# Cross-cultural experimental philosophy on knowledge, free will and moral responsibility

## Short answer

The finding that launched this literature has not survived replication. That finding was that Westerners and East or South Asians have different intuitions about knowledge. Larger multi-country studies have instead found striking similarity in the core patterns for both knowledge and free will.

The cultural variation that has held up, or at least not yet collapsed, has three features:

- It is mostly about degree rather than direction.
- It concerns how much weight people give particular factors.
- It is strongest for moral responsibility judgments in populations far from the university and online samples that dominate the field.

The live debate now is whether this "surprising stability" is real, or partly an artifact of whom researchers sample and how.

## 1. Knowledge

**The original claim.** Weinberg, Nichols and Stich (2001) drew on Nisbett's work on "holistic" versus "analytic" thinking. They gave Rutgers undergraduates a Gettier case:

- Bob believes his friend Jill drives an American car.
- Her Buick has been stolen and replaced by a Pontiac, also an American car.
- So Bob's belief is true, but only by luck.

About a quarter of Western-heritage students said Bob "really knows," versus a majority of East Asian- and South Asian-heritage students. Two details matter in hindsight:

- The "cultures" were US students sorted by self-reported background.
- Each Asian group had only about two dozen people.

The paper became a pillar of the "negative program." The argument ran: if epistemic intuitions vary by culture, why treat Western philosophers' intuitions as evidence about knowledge itself?

**What happened next.**

- **Direct replications failed.** Nagel, San Juan and Mar (2013) found Gettier cases judged as non-knowledge across ethnic groups in a diverse Toronto-area sample. Kim and Yuan (2015) and Seyedsayamdost (2015) found no cultural difference on the original vignette.
- **Large multi-site studies found the same pattern everywhere.** These were co-led by Machery and Stich himself, one of the original authors, through the Geography of Philosophy project. Majorities denied knowledge in Gettier cases in Brazil, India, Japan and the US ("Gettier Across Cultures," 2017). A follow-up found the same across roughly two dozen countries spanning South America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia. Magnitudes vary by case and site; the direction doesn't.
- **Stakes showed no effect either.** The same network found that practical stakes had little or no effect on knowledge attributions across many countries (Rose et al. 2019, "Nothing at Stake in Knowledge").
- **Other evidence converges.** Linguists in the Natural Semantic Metalanguage tradition argue that every language has a word for KNOW. Developmental and comparative work suggests that tracking what others *know* comes early, possibly before tracking what they *believe* (Phillips et al. 2021).

**What's still open.**

- Within a single culture, Gettier judgments depend on case details. Starmans and Friedman (2012) found people attributing knowledge when the evidence was "authentic." Nagel et al. and Turri (2013) found denial when the case structure was clear. So the variation that matters may be across vignettes, not cultures.
- Translation is a substantive choice, because many languages split English "know" across several verbs (know-that, be acquainted with, understand).
- As far as I know, Gettier-style cases have barely been tested in small-scale, non-literate societies.

**Verdict:** This is the best-known cross-cultural x-phi claim to fail replication. Among the populations studied, the evidence supports a shared core folk epistemology.

## 2. Free will and responsibility under determinism

**The US baseline is well replicated and depends heavily on framing.**

- Asked abstractly whether anyone in a deterministic universe could be fully morally responsible, most people say no.
- Shown a vivid, concrete wrongdoing in that same universe, most say the agent *is* responsible (Nichols & Knobe 2007).
- Descriptions of determinism that don't seem to bypass the agent's beliefs and desires get mostly compatibilist answers (Nahmias et al. 2006; Nahmias & Murray 2011).
- Which of these responses reflects confusion is still contested.

**Cross-culturally:**

- **Sarkissian et al. (2010)** ran the abstract version in the US, Hong Kong, India and Colombia, using modest university samples. The question was whether such intuitions reflect Western religious and philosophical traditions. Instead, in all four countries, majorities said our universe is indeterministic and that determinism rules out full moral responsibility.
- **Hannikainen et al. (2019)** surveyed about 5,300 people in 20 countries and 16 languages.
  - Overall, people ascribed responsibility even when the agent lacked alternative possibilities or wasn't the ultimate source of the action. This is the compatibilist-leaning pattern familiar from concrete US cases.
  - Culture changed one thing. Being the ultimate source of one's action boosted judgments of free will, control and blame for American, European and Middle Eastern participants. It mattered much less for Asian participants. The authors link this to known cultural differences in explaining behavior by disposition versus situation.
  - Everywhere, people who scored higher on cognitive reflection gave more incompatibilist answers.
- **Concept-level doubts.** Berniūnas et al. (2021, "The weirdness of belief in free will") used free-listing and prototype methods in several countries. They argue that "free will" in the philosophers' sense is a culturally specific concept that doesn't map neatly onto its translations. Wisniewski et al. (2019) found that across several countries, belief in free will tracked belief in mind–body dualism more closely than beliefs about determinism.

**Verdict:** Three basic patterns look stable across the cultures sampled:
- abstract incompatibilism;
- concrete compatibilism;
- belief that our world is indeterministic.

The most interesting cultural difference, the role of being the ultimate source, comes from one large study that hasn't been independently replicated. Whether the question even translates remains unresolved.

## 3. Moral responsibility: intent, outcome, and whom to blame

The strongest evidence for real variation is here, and it comes from very different samples.

- **Barrett et al. (2016, PNAS)** studied ten populations on six continents, eight of them small-scale societies.
  - Intent mattered a great deal in the Western comparison samples.
  - In some small-scale societies (e.g., Yasawa Island, Fiji), intentional and accidental harms were judged much more alike.
  - The weight given to mitigating factors also varied. These included self-defense, necessity, mistake of fact and insanity.
- **McNamara et al. (2019)** linked outcome-focused judgment in Fiji to local "opacity of mind" norms against speculating about others' thoughts. Ethnographers have documented such norms across parts of the Pacific.
- **Curtin et al. (2020)** found that societies with more intensive kinship systems placed less weight on mental states. This study largely draws on the same data.

These results are consistent, but they come from overlapping research teams with small samples per society. Two interpretive questions remain:
- Did people understand the "accidental" scenarios the same way?
- Do their judgments track blameworthiness, or obligations to compensate?

No independent large-scale replication exists, and one would be hard to run.

Outside x-phi proper, cultural psychologists have reported East–West differences in how much responsibility goes to groups, or to leaders "by proxy" (Menon et al. 1999; Zemba et al. 2006). These also haven't faced large-scale replication.

**Related moral-judgment work shows shared structure with varying levels.**

- Knobe's side-effect effect replicated across dozens of countries, both in Many Labs 2 and in the X-Phi Replicability Project. This is the finding that harmful side effects are judged more intentional than helpful ones.
- Awad et al. (2020) surveyed about 70,000 people in 42 countries. The same ranking of trolley variants appeared everywhere, while overall willingness to sacrifice one person to save five varied by country.
- Bago et al. (2022) tested 45 countries. The effect of using physical force on the victim appeared in every cultural cluster. Its interaction with intention was clear in Western clusters but inconclusive elsewhere.

My own reading: variation shows up on dimensions the early literature mostly didn't test (how much intent matters, whom to blame). It doesn't show up on the dimensions it did test (Gettier cases, determinism).

## 4. The replication picture as a whole

- **X-Phi Replicability Project (Cova et al. 2021).** It re-ran 40 studies, and about 70% replicated. That is well above the roughly 36–39% in the 2015 psychology reproducibility project. But studies that manipulated the *content* of cases replicated far more reliably than studies claiming *demographic* differences. Claimed gender differences in philosophical intuitions failed just as the cultural ones did (Seyedsayamdost 2015; Adleberg et al. 2015).
- **Many Labs 2.** Effects that replicated generally did so across 36 countries with little variation between samples. However, its effects weren't chosen to probe cultural differences.
- **Knobe (2021), "Philosophical Intuitions Are Surprisingly Stable Across Both Demographic Groups and Situations."** He synthesizes the pattern: content effects are robust, while effects of culture, gender, age and personality are mostly small or fragile.
- **Stich and Machery (2023) reply that this overreaches.**
  - They point to differences that have mostly held up. One is the Gödel case, where East Asian and Western participants differ in intuitions about how proper names refer, though what the difference means is disputed. Another is the small-scale-society results.
  - They also argue that the field's samples are too similar and too small to establish universality.

**Why did the early differences collapse? Mostly statistics.**
- Groups of a couple dozen people can only reliably detect differences of roughly 30–40 percentage points.
- So any significant result from such groups probably overstates the true gap.
- Reliably detecting a 10-point difference takes roughly 400 people per group.
- Add many vignettes, several groups and flexible analyses, and fragile positive results are expected.

## 5. Why "universal" should be held loosely

- **Sampling.** "Cross-cultural" in x-phi usually means students or online panelists in different countries. These people are educated, urban and globally connected: the WEIRD problem (Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan 2010). Barrett et al. show what can appear once you sample beyond them.
- **Stimuli.** Western philosophers designed the vignettes, which were then translated, and measurement equivalence is rarely checked. Abstract set-ups like "Universe A" are strange everywhere.
- **Absence of evidence.** Few studies use equivalence tests. "A majority denies knowledge everywhere" is compatible with 60% in one place and 85% in another.
- **Independence.** Much of the large-scale evidence for universality comes from one consortium. That work is careful, but it isn't independent replication.
- **Within beats between.** In nearly every sample, a substantial minority, often 15–40%, gives the "non-standard" answer. Disagreement within a culture typically dwarfs differences between cultures.

## 6. Philosophical upshot

The negative program lost its flagship premise for knowledge. The empirical challenge to the method of cases has mostly shifted to two targets:
- disagreement within a population;
- sensitivity to irrelevant features such as the order and framing of cases, where the replication record is itself mixed.

Universality wouldn't vindicate the intuitions anyway. Shared intuitions may reflect shared cognitive machinery, and shared machinery can produce shared errors. That is exactly why both sides of the free-will debate offer "error theories" of each other's intuitions.

A tentative synthesis, which is my interpretation:
- Judgments close to basic social cognition look largely shared. Examples: whether a true belief was true only by luck, or whether a choice was "up to" someone.
- Judgments shaped by social institutions vary more. Examples: how much intent should matter, or who answers for a harm.

**Bottom line:** For knowledge and free will, the best summary is "surprisingly similar, at least among the people we've asked." For moral responsibility, the clearest variation concerns how intentions and outcomes are weighed. It appears precisely when researchers move beyond the usual populations.

**Good entry points:** read Knobe (2021) together with Stich and Machery's (2023) reply. Cova et al. (2021) covers replication, and Barrett et al. (2016) makes the strongest case for variation.

I'm working from memory with a training cutoff, so check exact figures against the papers and look for newer multi-site studies.

# Can There Be Objective Moral Facts in a Purely Physical Universe?

**Short answer:** it depends on how much "objective" has to mean. The strongest kind of moral objectivity is hard to fit into a strictly physical world. A substantial kind fits fine. And the *feeling* that some things are really wrong can be partly explained, which is not the same as explaining it away.

Your question bundles three questions, and each needs a different tool:

1. **Metaphysical:** can facts about what we ought to do exist if everything supervenes on the physical? This is settled by argument and coherence.
2. **Conceptual:** what separates "really wrong" from "merely disliked"? This is settled by clarification.
3. **Explanatory:** why does wrongness *feel* like a demand rather than a taste? This is settled by evidence from psychology.

## 1. Tighten the terms

**"Purely physical"** usually means that everything supervenes on the physical. It doesn't mean the only real facts are ones stated in the vocabulary of physics. Health, money, a valid inference and an unsafe bridge appear nowhere in the Standard Model, yet few physicalists deny they're real. So the question isn't whether wrongness is a property of particles. It's whether *normative* facts, facts about what there is reason to do, can be among the higher-level facts.

**"Objective"** comes in grades:
- **(a)** Independent of any one person's attitudes. "This bridge is unsafe" is true however you feel about it.
- **(b)** Independent of *everyone's* attitudes, even idealized ones.
- **(c)** Categorically binding. It gives a reason to any agent at all, whatever that agent wants. Mackie called this "to-be-pursuedness."

Most of the fight is about (c). And "merely disliked" is a false binary. There's a large middle ground between "built into the cosmos" and "like my distaste for broccoli."

## 2. The strongest case for "no"

- **Is/ought (Hume):** no pile of descriptive facts entails an "ought" unless one of the premises is already an "ought."
- **Queerness (Mackie 1977):** an objective prescription would be a fact with demanding force built into it. That would be unlike anything else we know of, and it's unclear what faculty could detect it.
- **Explanatory idleness (Harman 1977):** you see kids setting a cat on fire and judge "wrong." Your psychology fully explains that judgment, so the wrongness itself seems to do no causal work.
- **The Darwinian dilemma (Street 2006):** evolution shaped our evaluative dispositions for fitness, not truth. If moral facts are independent of us, either selection somehow tracked them (there's little reason to think so) or our agreement with them is a coincidence.

Together these make grade-(c) objectivity in a purely physical universe look somewhere between mysterious and unmotivated. The arguments are strong. Whether they're decisive is the live dispute.

## 3. The strongest cases for "yes," or "yes, in the sense that matters"

**Naturalist realism** (Railton, Boyd, Sturgeon)
- **The claim:** moral properties are natural properties, roughly what promotes or frustrates the flourishing of beings who can fare well or badly. They're real in the way health is real.
- **Reply to Harman:** Sturgeon argued moral facts do explain things. For example, the particular injustice of American slavery helps explain why abolitionism arose when and where it did.
- **Weakness:** the normativity objection (Moore, Parfit). Even if goodness just *is* what promotes flourishing, why does that fact give *me* a reason? The identification seems to leave out exactly the "ought."

**Non-naturalist realism** (Parfit, Scanlon, Enoch, Shafer-Landau)
- **The claim:** normative truths are like mathematical truths. They aren't located in spacetime and don't cause anything, but they aren't spooky either.
- **Honest note:** this partly *rejects* your premise, unless "purely physical" only means that every concrete thing is physical.
- **Strongest card, companions in guilt (Cuneo 2007):** epistemic norms are normative too. "You ought to believe what the evidence supports" is no more physical than "you ought not torture." If irreducible oughts can't exist in a physical world, the skeptic's own conclusion, that you *should* abandon moral realism, loses its force.
- **Responses:** one can treat epistemic oughts as conditional ("if you want truth, then..."). Even so, I find this the hardest point to wave away.

**Constructivism** (Korsgaard 1996, Scanlon's contractualism, Street's Humean version)
- **The claim:** objectivity isn't discovered out there. It's built into the standpoint of agency itself.
- **Korsgaard's version:** if you value anything, you're committed to valuing your own capacity to confer value. You can't consistently deny that standing to others relevantly like you.
- **Weakness:** this may deliver only "binding on agents who reason consistently," not grade (c). Street openly accepts this: an ideally coherent Caligula, someone who values cruelty with perfect consistency, escapes the argument.

**Valence realism** (Rawlette 2016; the Sidgwick tradition)
- I think this one fits physicalism most naturally.
- **The claim:** the badness of agony isn't inferred. It's presented in the experience itself, because pain is felt *as* to-be-avoided. If consciousness is physical, then some physical states are intrinsically bad for whoever has them.
- **Why it matters:** the "ought" doesn't have to be smuggled across Hume's gap, because it was never on the other side. It's already in what the experience is like.
- **The key step:** getting from "bad for me" to "bad, full stop, and a reason for you too" requires impartiality. Nothing about the agony's being *mine* is what makes it matter.
- **Weaknesses:** egoists resist exactly that step (Sidgwick's "dualism of practical reason"). The view also grounds a welfare core more easily than it grounds promising, honesty or rights, though those can plausibly be read as structures that protect welfare and agency.

**Quasi-realism** (Blackburn, Gibbard)
- This matters most for your second question.
- **The claim:** even if there are no robust moral facts, moral judgments aren't reports of dislike. You can coherently say "kicking dogs would be wrong even if everyone approved of it."
- **Why that's not cheating:** that sentence is itself a commitment about *what matters*: the dog's pain, not anyone's approval. On this view, "really wrong" is something you can earn the right to say without inflating your metaphysics.

**Theistic grounding** (Adams; the Euthyphro problem)
- This rejects the premise entirely. Many people take the difficulty of housing morality in a physical world as evidence *against* physicalism.
- That relocates the problem rather than dissolving it: is God's nature good simply because it's God's?

**For calibration:** in the PhilPapers 2020 survey, about 62% of philosophers accepted or leaned toward moral realism, and about 26% toward anti-realism. That's informative, but it isn't a verdict. The survey can't tell you which realism is right, or whether it's compatible with strict physicalism.

## 4. Why wrongness *feels* objective

This part is empirical and well studied.

- **It's built into moral thinking early.** From around ages 3–4, children judge hitting wrong even if the teacher allows it, and wrong at other schools too. They judge talking without raising your hand fine if the teacher allows it (Turiel 1983; Nucci; Smetana). Independence from authority is part of the *form* of moral judgment. The core findings are robust; how far they hold across cultures is contested (Haidt, Koller & Dias 1993; Kelly et al. 2007).
- **Ordinary people's views about morality's status are mixed.** People treat some moral claims, especially gratuitous harm, almost like facts, and others more like preferences (Goodwin & Darley 2008). Relativist intuitions grow when people imagine judges from very different cultures or species (Sarkissian et al. 2011). The strong sense is strongest for harm and fairness.
- **It does a job.** A judgment that presents itself as binding works as a commitment device (Joyce 2006). "That's wrong" resists self-serving renegotiation and coordinates groups far better than "I'd rather you didn't." Hume described this as the mind "gilding or staining all natural objects with the colours borrowed from internal sentiment."

## 5. Explaining is not explaining away

This is the crucial step. Our belief that 2 + 2 = 4 has an evolutionary history, and so does vision, and both track real things. A story about where a belief came from only debunks it if the process that produced it was *insensitive to whether it's true*. So debunking is selective:

- **"Gratuitous agony is bad"** has a plausible common-cause story (Enoch 2010). Selection made us averse to pain because pain tracks bodily damage, and pain is also genuinely bad for whoever feels it. The belief and the fact share a root, so their match isn't a coincidence.
- **Purity, in-group and sexual-taboo intuitions** are where debunking bites hard, and history confirms it. The felt objectivity was fully present in condemnations of interracial marriage and homosexuality. **Feeling that something is really wrong does not certify that it is.**

That gives a usable test: does a particular sense of wrongness survive learning where it came from? Wrongness grounded in someone's suffering or violated agency usually does. Wrongness grounded in disgust, or in "that's not how we do things," often doesn't.

## 6. Where I come down

This is my considered lean, not a settled result.

- **The strongest grade, (c), I can't see how to secure in a strictly physical world** without something like non-naturalism, which bends the premise. The companions-in-guilt argument keeps me from calling it refuted.
- **A substantial objectivity survives physicalism comfortably.**
  - Suffering and flourishing are as physical as anything else.
  - Their badness and goodness are encountered from the inside, not projected from outside.
  - Impartiality, meaning refusing to let "mine" do work it can't justify, carries that badness across persons.
  - That secures grade (a) and much of grade (b): wrongness that doesn't depend on what you or your culture happens to feel.
- **What grounds the strong sense, then?**
  - *Causally:* evolved and cultural moral thinking that represents norms as independent of authority.
  - *Rationally, where it's earned:* the sense is *about* something real and not about you, namely the victim's experience.
- **"Merely disliked" fails on every view, including the deflationary ones.** Your dislike of broccoli doesn't claim to concern anyone else's welfare. It doesn't demand consistency across similar cases. And it wouldn't be undone by learning the broccoli enjoyed being eaten.

One bridge worth flagging, since the framework you're working in treats the self as a constructed model. Parfit (*Reasons and Persons*, Part III) argued that if personal identity isn't the deep further fact it seems to be, egoism loses its privileged status, and the impartiality step above gets *easier*. That is the analytic cousin of the Īśā Upaniṣad's "one who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, shrinks from none" (verse 6). The metaphysical version stays at the horizon. Parfit's version is an argument you can check. It's defensible and contested.

## Threads to pull

- **Companions in guilt:** does abandoning moral oughts drag epistemic oughts down with it? I think this is where the debate actually turns.
- **From "bad for me" to "bad, full stop":** is impartiality rationally required, or just one coherent option among several?
- **The genealogy test, run on yourself:** which of your own strongest moral convictions survive learning where they came from?

# What Would It Mean for a Far More Capable AI to Be Aligned With Human Values?

The phrase "aligned with human values" pictures those values as a magnetic north, with the AI as a compass needle. Your question takes the north away.
